title: Ultra-highfield neuroimaging for the multimodal investigation of neuroplasticity-related effects of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
summary:
Electroconvulsive therapy is one of the most effective treatments for severe treatmnt resistant depression. However, it is still not well understood why it works so well. It is known that certain areas of the brain become slightly larger after treatment, but it is unclear how these changes come about and whether they are linked to the improvement of depression.
In this study, we examine people with depression who are receiving electroconvulsive therapy as part of their regular care. Using a particularly precise magnetic resonance scanner, we take images of the brain at three points in time: before the first treatment, after the first treatment and at the end of the treatment series. We measure the amount of certain neurotransmitters in the brain, how well different brain areas work together and how the brain is structured. We also use interviews, questionnaires and short attention and memory tests to record how symptoms change over time.
Our aim is to better understand how electroconvulsive therapy works in the brain. In the long term, this could help to predict early who will benefit from the treatment. The study does not affect the treatment itself.
